name: Adam Tanaka

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, parties or government. Your answers are confidential. What is an ordinary working day like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am Adam, 27, and I lead a tax review team at an accounting firm. I have a master’s degree and a chartered accountancy qualification, and I spend mornings checking returns against bank records before clients start calling. I like teaching a junior how to spot a bad figure, but the late-season hours pile up.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How are you placed financially, and what tools do you use?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My pay is typical for this job and Samira, my partner, works in a library, so we can cover rent. I have about four months of expenses saved and there are some similar accounting jobs nearby. I have never used AI tools; I want to see a clear audit trail before anything touches a client return.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could live with a quieter version of the present. Tax deadlines and my team would still set the pace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell colleagues that receipt sorting is fine if we can trace every entry back to a document. The client must still be able to ask which person checked the return.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ordinary workload worries me more than this version of AI. My salary is typical for a senior accountant and I have about four months of expenses saved, but I am tired of unpaid late evenings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the current review rota and continue doing the final checks myself. Starting with the next tax season, I would ask my manager Ruth to record our overtime and pay it or give time back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel mostly steady about my job and rent in this picture. I still resent carrying extra hours while the firm calls them professional commitment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try the receipt tool yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not yet; I have never used an AI tool, and I prefer the method I can explain to a client. If a trained colleague finds a reliable way to check it, I will look at that evidence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say if Ruth refuses overtime pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would bring our rota and logged hours to the staff association with two colleagues. That is a work condition we can ask about together, even without any AI shock.

say: I would tell colleagues **receipt sorting** is acceptable only when every figure can be traced.
I would say a **named reviewer** still owes clients an explanation.
think: My typical salary and **four-month reserve** keep rent covered for now.
I am more bothered by **unpaid overtime** than modest software changes.
do: Keep our **review rota** and final checks in place.
Bring logged **overtime hours** to the staff association if Ruth refuses pay.
feel: I feel **calm** about income but irritated by late hours.
S0.quote: The client must still be able to ask which person checked the return.
fieldNote: He connects his caution about AI to **traceable client work** rather than a claim that small tools cannot function.
His moderate savings keep the plateau **financially manageable**, while unpaid hours remain a separate complaint.

steps.text: Keep the current client review rota and final checks
Bring logged overtime to the staff association if unpaid

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can hear the junior desks getting quieter before the firm announces any change. Our review work is nearly all on screens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell staff that the firm must show which checks the software performs and which posts it plans to fill. A senior title should not be an excuse to make us supervise twice as many returns without help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In private, I think my own review role could shrink as the software takes writing and checking. Four months of savings buys time, but there are only some similar firms nearby and I would not enjoy starting over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask Ruth and the staff association for a paid pilot with a human sign-off rule and a staffing report each quarter. I would keep my manual review for now; if the pilot shows reliable results, I would take a supervised class on the chosen system during paid hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious because our regular work is precisely the work being moved. The savings give me a little room to argue, not a guarantee of a new post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the pilot credible to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would want twenty old returns with known errors and a record of what the tool misses. I would not put a live client file through it to satisfy a sales claim.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would join you at the association?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask two other team leads to bring the hours and vacancy figures. If the firm will not show those numbers, we cannot judge whether the new targets are fair.

say: I would seek a **paid pilot** with human sign-off and a quarterly staffing report.
I would ask the firm to show how its software handles **known errors**.
think: My **review role** may shrink even if I am senior.
Four months saved and **some nearby firms** give me time, not certainty.
do: Gather **vacancy figures** with two team leads for the staff association.
Take a **supervised class** on the chosen system during paid hours if the pilot works.
feel: I feel **anxious** about losing hours or the team role.
S1.quote: Four months of savings buys time, but there are only some similar firms nearby and I would not enjoy starting over.
fieldNote: He favors **collective scrutiny** of staffing before using the system; he has never used AI himself.
His willingness to learn is **conditional** on a proven pilot and paid supervised instruction.

steps.text: Bring vacancy and hours figures to the staff association
Take paid supervised training if the chosen system passes pilot

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is almost no notice for a profession built on long training. Robots arriving later do nothing for my desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the firm to publish a transition plan for staff and clients now, with a human answer to every disputed return. I would ask the staff association to press for severance terms before a rush of cuts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my review job or most of its hours to go when cheaper thinking work arrives in 2028. My four-month reserve is real, but a gap longer than that would put my rent and partner Samira under pressure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I would transfer a fixed small amount from my ordinary salary into savings each month. I would join the staff association meeting on severance this month; if the post ends in the first year after 2028, I would apply for an advertised tax appeals role with a published salary and use severance if the firm offers it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed because this could erase the work I was trained to do before I can build a second skill. I do have a plan, but it depends on a real opening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Samira tonight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my partner Samira that we should not sign a more expensive lease next spring. I would say my income could stop even though hers would still cover part of the bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for a new qualification?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, not with two years and a four-month reserve. I would ask the firm to fund tax appeals training before cuts, but I would not enrol unless the paid place actually exists.

say: I would call for **severance terms** and a published staff transition plan.
I would say AGI reaches our **tax desks** in 2028; robots around 2031 are irrelevant to that loss.
think: I expect a major **hours cut** or job loss in 2028.
A **four-month reserve** would run out if a posted appeals vacancy does not appear.
do: Transfer a fixed **salary amount** into savings each month.
Join the association’s **severance meeting** this month.
Apply for a **published-salary appeals post** after 2028 if my role ends.
feel: I feel **alarmed** by likely lost pay and an uncertain vacancy.
S2.quote: My four-month reserve is real, but a gap longer than that would put my rent and partner Samira under pressure.
fieldNote: He expects a **2028 screen-work loss**, years before capable robots arrive.
He declines speculative self-funded study; the appeals move needs a **real salaried vacancy** and possibly severance.

steps.text: Transfer a fixed amount from monthly salary into savings
Join the staff association meeting on severance terms
Apply for advertised salaried tax appeals posts if job ends

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is enough to organise, though it does not make the work safe. I could use several tax seasons to see which duties remain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell colleagues that a five-year runway should be written into staffing agreements, not left to promises. Our desks face AGI in 2031, and robots around 2034 are a separate matter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I still think the checking role might disappear, but I could grow my savings beyond four months. I could also learn the appeals process through paid casework before any new job is needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would ask Ruth for one paid appeals case each quarter and enrol in the professional body’s tax disputes module if the firm covers the fee. In the first year after 2031 I would try to move to the firm’s appeals unit if it has a salaried opening; otherwise I would keep my current pay as long as the work remains.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious but less pressed than with 2028. Five years before AGI arrives in 2031 would let me test a new path before resigning for a rumour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the union ask for over those years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would support a written commitment to paid learning time and notice before posts are removed. The staff association can take those terms to Ruth each year with the vacancy figures.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the firm will not pay the course fee?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would use its free case library and postpone the module rather than spend my rent buffer. I might ask a nearby firm about an actual appeals opening, but I would not hand in notice without salary terms.

say: I would seek **written notice** and paid learning time before posts disappear.
I would say **2031** threatens account checking before robots arrive around 2034.
think: Five years could build **savings** and real appeals experience without gambling my rent.
do: Enrol in a **tax disputes module** if the firm pays its fee.
Take one **paid appeals case** each quarter if Ruth agrees.
Move into a **salaried appeals opening** after 2031 if one exists.
feel: I feel **anxious**, with time to test a path.
S3.quote: Five years before AGI arrives in 2031 would let me test a new path before resigning for a rumour.
fieldNote: His retraining requires a **funded module** and paid casework, not merely asking for a budget.
He keeps a **salary condition** on the appeals move and retains his current post if no opening exists.

steps.text: Enrol in tax disputes module if firm pays course fee
Bring paid-learning and notice terms to staff association
Move to salaried appeals opening after 2031 if available

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is a long time in a young career. I would use it carefully, without telling trainees their future is settled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the firm has a decade to keep training junior accountants and create a fair path into new work. AGI reaches our screen work in 2036, while hands-on robots around 2039 change little about tax returns.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In private I expect preparation fees to fall, but at 37 I could have several years of appeals experience and more savings. I still want the work to serve clients, and I will not leave a stable wage for an unpriced title.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep leading the review team now and ask Ruth for paid appeals cases, taking one each tax season only if she approves. I would transfer a fixed amount from ordinary salary into savings until I have six months of expenses; in the first year after 2036 I would take a salaried client disputes role if one is posted and my team role contracts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy rather than alarmed because ten years could give me an honest choice. It would still hurt to see our trainees lose the chance to learn on real files.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask for a policy change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the staff association to press for a funded trainee route and a notice period before any automated cut. I would bring actual trainee and vacancy counts, not a speech about the future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where do you see yourself if no disputes post opens?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the accounting work I am paid for while it exists and use the six-month reserve if the firm cuts it. I would look at some nearby firms, but only apply to vacancies with clear duties and wages.

say: I would seek a **funded trainee route** and notice before automated cuts.
I would explain that **2036** affects tax desks before robots arrive around 2039.
think: Preparation **fees** may fall, but ten years could build appeals skill and cash.
I will not trade a **stable wage** for an unpriced job title.
do: Take **paid appeals cases** each tax season only if Ruth approves.
Save a fixed **salary amount** until six months of expenses are covered.
Take a **salaried disputes role** after 2036 only if my team post contracts.
feel: I feel **uneasy**, with room to prepare and protect trainees.
S4.quote: I will not leave a stable wage for an unpriced title.
fieldNote: A ten-year runway lets him build **experience and reserves** while remaining wary of unproven software.
His support for **trainee protections** is concrete: funding and notice tied to vacancy counts.

steps.text: Keep leading review; take paid appeals cases only if Ruth approves
Save a fixed salary amount until six months of expenses are covered
Seek funded trainee route through staff association
Take salaried disputes role after 2036 if team post contracts

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because our screen-based review could vanish before I learn another paid role. Severance agreed in advance, paid appeals training, and an income bridge after a cut would help. I would also want real vacancies with salaries attached, not a list of hopeful job names.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask what happens to the juniors who learn by checking real mistakes. A firm cannot claim to value judgment while removing every place where someone learns it. I would fight for their training even if my own post survived.

headlineQuote: A firm cannot claim to value judgment while removing every place where someone learns it.
portrait: Adam is a **27-year-old** team lead with a master’s degree and chartered qualification who prepares tax returns.
He has **typical pay**, four months of savings, a partner, and some nearby accounting firms.
He has **never used AI** and wants a traceable review process before testing client work.
He favours **staff association** action on overtime, severance, learning time, and funded trainee routes.
The **2028** shock alarms him; longer warning lets him build reserves and paid appeals experience.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove his screen-based review role before he gains another paid position.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **agreed severance**, paid appeals training, an income bridge, and real posted vacancies with salaries.
